Please read /papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/notes/55_VCD_GT_CM_ANALYTICAL_MANUSCRIPT_CONTINUATION_20261118.md. I want to understand the current research, and brainstorm paths forward. Can you explain at a high level the most recent developments, with enough background that I can follow, referencing the manuscript where necessary?

Please place any notes in the brainstorm folder, and record chat history in the chat-histories folder.

I’ll read the continuation note, the manuscript sections it points to, and the project’s results and caution summaries. Then I’ll explain where the research stands and which next steps look promising, with any new notes saved in the brainstorm folder.

The main development is a rigorous way to approximate the evolving system over a whole time interval. The recent work also identifies a practical limit: the tested error bounds are still too large for that approximation to be useful. Separately, better handling of shared errors has sharpened the existing local calculation. I’m tracing how these results connect to the larger goal of controlling zero collisions.

The key distinction is now clear: the manuscript proves that a finite model can follow the true system, but that alone does not show a gap stays open. The most useful next question seems to be how to preserve shared errors and cancellations all the way to the final gap bound. The recent local improvements show that this can make a measurable difference.

I’ll save a reading guide and a ranked set of questions. I’d prioritize a bound tailored to the final gap or transport quantity, using the shared source errors throughout. A useful test would show whether that closes the existing error budget or extends the certified region; further narrowing an already positive interval would be a smaller gain.

The research now has **a proved framework for approximating the evolving zero system and sharper local gap bounds**. The main unresolved problem is making those estimates practical and extending them to every potentially closing gap.

I read Note55 against the current manuscript and progress register. The manuscript’s results have internal assessment within their stated hypotheses; they have not had independent specialist review.

To understand the project, start with the Newman heat family \(H(t,z)\). At \(t=0\), having all its zeros real is equivalent to RH. The de Bruijn–Newman constant \(\Lambda\) marks the time above which all zeros are real. RH says \(\Lambda\le0\), while Rodgers and Tao proved \(\Lambda\ge0\). This project seeks control that would let us descend from an established all-real time and improve an upper bound. [Rodgers–Tao](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05914v5)

As time decreases, two real zeros can meet and become a nonreal conjugate pair. The manuscript follows a pair using its center \(c\) and a signed quantity \(D\):

- \(D>0\): two distinct real zeros, with gap \(2\sqrt D\).
- \(D=0\): a merger.
- \(D<0\): a nonreal conjugate pair.

Its central equation is

\[
D'=2-4DM.
\]

Here \(M\) collects the influence of **all the other zeros**. The pair’s own interaction contributes the \(2\); the surrounding zeros modify its motion through \(M\). These coordinates remain well behaved at a merger, making them useful for studying the event. [Manuscript §1](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/01_framework.tex)

The difficulty is that \(M\) also evolves. Its equation involves higher moments of the exterior zeros, whose equations involve still higher moments. That produces the infinite hierarchy. The complex-\(p\) construction extends the moment exponent to complex values and supplies contour representations. The recent work has broadened into the question of how to approximate and use this whole coupled system.

**Three recent developments matter most.**

1. **One finite model can now follow the system over an entire interval.**

   Take finitely many zeros at the initial time, build their polynomial, and evolve that same polynomial by the heat equation. The manuscript proves an error rate of \(O(\log N/N)\), with fixed height, interval and derivative order; \(N\) is the initial zero cutoff.

   This is stronger than finding a fresh approximation at each time. All the model’s moments remain compatible because they come from one actual polynomial. The error can then be transferred to the pair coordinates, exterior interaction and transport quantities.

   The qualification is substantial: the theorem requires initial data and independently verified contours isolating the pair. Its constants need not be affordable, and it does not yet give an efficient approximation using only a few moments. [§6](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/20_common_time_approximation.tex), [§7](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/21_counted_transfer.tex)

2. **The latest work identifies why the tested practical implementation fails.**

   The original absolute error estimate loses an enormous amount by measuring everything from the origin. A revised estimate centers near the pair and accounts for the full Gaussian propagation, including its tails.

   That repair helps, but the resulting bound still misses the chosen transport accuracy of \(10^{-6}\), even under the very large cutoff allowance \(N\le2^{40}\). Consequently, that particular approach has been parked.

   This means **the error estimate is too pessimistic for its intended use**. It does not establish that the actual approximation is inaccurate or that every finite method is impractical. The distinction suggests looking for cancellations and correlated errors that the absolute estimate discards. [§8](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/23_conditioning.tex)

3. **Preserving shared errors has already improved the direct local calculation.**

   Several quantities are extracted from the same underlying function values. Their errors therefore cannot vary independently in every possible worst-case direction. Retaining this dependence produces smaller certified intervals.

   The recent sequence includes:

   | Improvement | Recorded effect |
   |---|---|
   | Shared errors between two moment readouts | More than 6.40% narrower than the corresponding independent-moment bound |
   | Sharper interpolation error estimate | More than 33.94-fold narrowing of the preceding centered interval |
   | Joint analytic constraint on contour errors | A proved further reduction exceeding 2.4% of the complete interval width; the new endpoint artifact remains unexecuted |

   These use different comparison baselines, so their percentages should not be combined. They improve the direct calculation itself. [§20](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/22_correlated_enclosures.tex)

The existing certificate protects one pair near \(x=14010.1\) throughout \([-0.0003,0.1]\), with minimum \(D\) approximately \(0.000822>0\). That is meaningful local coverage. Further narrowing its uncertainty does not automatically protect another pair or extend the interval. [Appendix B](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/16_supporting_compact_example.tex)

For brainstorming, **my strongest preference is to estimate the final gap quantity while preserving common errors throughout the calculation**.

For example, a common multiplicative normalization disappears from \(H_z/H\). Bounding the numerator and denominator separately can lose that cancellation. The research question is whether such dependence can be retained through the whole time evolution, contour extraction and final gap estimate. A useful success would be meeting the existing transport tolerance or certifying a longer interval at the same source budget. The manuscript’s forward–adjoint formulation provides an existing framework for this, but its complete error terms still need useful bounds. [§19](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/19_two_sided_refinement.tex)

Two further questions seem worthwhile:

- **Can compatibility stabilize a small hierarchy?** Moments arising from one divisor obey relations that independent error intervals ignore. A small, realizable model might exploit these relations, but it needs a bound on accumulated error over a full interval.
- **Can block information protect the smallest gap?** Controlling a block’s total length does not stop one interior gap closing while others widen. The next geometric advance would control every eligible gap, including boundary influences and transitions between counted regions. Conserved quantities may help organize this, but a positive quartic invariant alone can coexist with collision.

The broader challenge is joining compact-region results to high-height estimates on a common time interval, with no omitted exceptional gaps. The manuscript’s [§21](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/07_discussion.tex) is the best short account of that remaining gap.

I saved the fuller explanation, reading order and collision-control screen in [brainstorm Note06](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/brainstorm/notes/06_VCD_GT_CM_RESEARCH_POSITION_AND_PATHS_DISCUSSION_20261118.md). This conversation is registered in the brainstorm’s [chat-histories folder](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/brainstorm/chat-histories/README.md), with capture of this final reply arranged.

I’ll check how the manuscript treats the two pole exponents and \(\sqrt D\), then clarify what I meant by estimating the final gap. I’ll also revisit the earlier localization discussion to see whether the current results give that idea a more concrete role.

You’re right: I underplayed the \(p,q\) structure. Section 3 treats the two poles separately, using \(c\pm\sqrt D\), and Section 4 carries that structure into the coupled lattice. The proved split-pole recurrence uses integer \(p,q\); the complex-exponent result is a separate part of the manuscript. I also found the earlier Pestun discussion, which makes a useful distinction between a cancellation identity and a cancellation derived from an actual localization complex.

The localization connection is useful because it suggests a stronger question than “does a common factor cancel?”: can a symmetry explain which contributions to the gap cancel and identify what survives? One limitation matters here: a factor can disappear from the instantaneous zero readout yet still affect how those zeros move under heat flow. I’m separating those two roles in the notes.

I’ve corrected the overview and saved the follow-up. The sharper research question is whether a derived Ward identity can preserve cancellations through the full gap evolution. The existing contour formulas already give exact cancellations at a fixed time; the unresolved step is turning those into useful control over an interval.

You’re right: **I underplayed \(p,q\), and the \(\sqrt D\) geometry is central.** It is already present in the manuscript, especially §§3–4; my explanation should have foregrounded it.

Writing the target zeros as \(z_\pm=c\pm s\), with \(s=\sqrt D\), the split moments are
\[
P_{p,q}=\sum_{\rho_j\text{ exterior}}
\frac{1}{(\rho_j-c-s)^p(\rho_j-c+s)^q}.
\]
The two exponents probe the exterior relative to **each member of the pair separately**. Changing the sign of \(s\) exchanges the poles and therefore exchanges \(p,q\). This matters near a merger: labeled quantities can have square-root singularities, while suitable symmetric and divided-antisymmetric combinations remain regular. The complete \(S_n,T_n\) hierarchy retains this information in different coordinates. [Manuscript §3](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/03_split_poles.tex)

There is an important qualification: the manuscript proves the split hierarchy for **integer \(p,q\)**. Its complex-exponent theorem separately extends the power of the combined denominator \((w^2-D)^{-p}\). I did not find an established joint continuation with two independently complex exponents. So the two-index structure is central already; a full complex-\((p,q)\) theory remains a further question. [Manuscript §9](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/04_complex_powers.tex)

By **“estimating the final gap quantity,”** I meant bounding the uncertainty in
\[
D(t_*)=\frac{(z_+(t_*)-z_-(t_*))^2}{4},
\]
or obtaining a lower bound for \(\min_{t\in I}D(t)\) when protecting an entire interval. “Final” meant the quantity we ultimately need—not just the last time in the interval.

A simple example explains the preference. Suppose the roots are \(a-1\) and \(a+1\), with considerable uncertainty in \(a\). Their individual locations are uncertain, but their gap is exactly \(2\), and \(D=1\). Carrying their shared uncertainty through the subtraction preserves that fact. Bounding the two locations independently can lose it.

The normalization example is the same principle. On a zero-free contour, if
\[
\widetilde H=H(1+\varepsilon),
\qquad
\frac{\widetilde H_z}{\widetilde H}-\frac{H_z}{H}
=\frac{\varepsilon_z}{1+\varepsilon}.
\]
A spatially constant multiplicative error has no effect on this observable. The research question is whether we can preserve similarly useful dependencies through the evolution and obtain a better **complete error bound for \(D\)**. The recent correlated-enclosure results are already concrete examples of this principle. [Manuscript §20](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/22_correlated_enclosures.tex)

Your Pestun connection is worth revisiting. In that calculation, a \(Q\)-complex pairs fluctuation modes, and the surviving determinant is governed by an equivariant kernel/cokernel character of a transversally elliptic operator. The equivariant index carries substantially more information than one integer. That provides a concrete model for deriving cancellations from structure before estimating the surviving contributions. [Pestun, §4.4](https://arxiv.org/html/0712.2824v3)

Our [earlier localization discussion](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/weil-positivity/susy-positivity/investigations/wilson-loewner/notes/LOCALIZATION_AND_THE_POLE_CANCELLATION_20260920.md) reached a specific unresolved point: it could reproduce a gamma/pole factor through auxiliary bosonic and fermionic factors, but their spectrum was prescribed to match the desired expression. It had not derived that spectrum from an independently specified supercharge or localization complex.

The present results give that question a more concrete target:

- We have an exact two-pole observable and its complete exterior forcing.
- We have a compatible finite heat model on which a proposed identity could first be examined.
- We have demonstrated that retaining common dependencies improves actual error bounds.

My preferred initial investigation would therefore be **to seek a derived Ward identity for the full two-pole observable or its evolution error**, starting with that finite model. We would identify which contributions pair and cancel, what survives, and whether the surviving expression admits a useful bound. That would connect your localization idea directly to my preference for estimating the gap itself.

One distinction is crucial. An analytic nonvanishing factor can disappear from the contour readout of the pair **at a fixed time**, while still influencing its subsequent motion under heat flow. Exterior zeros enter \(D'=2-4DM\). Thus the desired identity must account for the exterior dynamics. Also, physical heat time changes \(D\); it cannot simply be identified with a localization deformation under which the observable is invariant.

An ordinary root-count index alone would not settle the problem: the count remains two when two roots merge. But that does **not** dismiss a richer equivariant construction. The earlier event-index work on \((H,H_z)\) already illustrates that distinction; its unresolved issue is the quantitative transfer to the required gap control.

I’ve corrected the overview and saved these distinctions, the earlier connections, and the exploratory proposal in [the brainstorm follow-up](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/brainstorm/notes/07_VCD_GT_CM_SPLIT_POLES_OBSERVABLES_AND_LOCALIZATION_20261118.md). Chat-history capture has been refreshed and arranged for this reply.

Comments:

- I'm ok with integer p, q - it seems that might be the more natural home for those variables. Perhaps it is worth foregrounding that in the manuscript, because originally we were looking into complex p, q.
- Regarding the discussion around "**estimating the final gap quantity",** I am thinking about the gaps as a chain. In fact I've been considering trying to express M in terms of the summed gaps, or in other ways. One way to think about it is as a dipole moment, as you get farther away it gets weaker, and M averages the dipole over all the external zeros. Higher orders actually are more sensitive to closer zeros, from what I can tell. This is my current intuition. 
- Please elaborate on this sentence: "An analytic nonvanishing factor can disappear from the contour readout of the pair **at a fixed time**, while still influencing its subsequent motion under heat flow"

I’ll check how the manuscript expresses the shared gap chain, work through your dipole interpretation of \(M\), and explain the nonvanishing-factor point with an explicit heat-flow example. I’ll also make a small manuscript clarification that foregrounds the integer \(p,q\) hierarchy.

Your chain picture is already an exact part of §4: \(M\) is written in terms of cumulative sums of the gaps to the left and right. The dipole intuition also has a precise form—each exterior zero contributes a difference of reciprocal distances to the two target zeros. I’ll use that to connect the chain picture, the stronger emphasis on nearby zeros at higher orders, and the heat-flow explanation.

The key distinction is now clear: a nonconstant factor leaves the pair’s positions unchanged at that instant, but changes the derivatives at those zeros, which determine their heat-flow velocities. In the simple polynomial example I’m checking, the same initial pair has \(D'=2\) by itself and \(D'=5/3\) with exterior zeros at \(\pm5\). The manuscript clarification has also compiled successfully.

The calculations check out, and the revised manuscript is still 107 pages with a clean build. The useful connection is that \(M\) measures how much the exterior field varies across a pair: common motion drops out, while the difference in the two velocities changes the gap. The notes now explain this both through cumulative gaps and through the local analytic factor.

I’ve foregrounded **integer \(p,q\)** in the manuscript’s abstract and introduction. Their rational algebra is central to the proved hierarchy; the later complex exponent is now clearly identified as a separate extension.

Your **chain picture is exact**, and I should have brought it into the explanation earlier. When the complete zero set is real and ordered, take a target gap \(g_n=x_{n+1}-x_n\). Let \(L_m\) and \(R_m\) denote the sums of the first \(m\) neighboring gaps to its left and right. Then
\[
M_n=\sum_{m\ge1}
\left[
\frac{1}{L_m(L_m+g_n)}
+\frac{1}{R_m(R_m+g_n)}
\right].
\]
This is already the “All-gap expression” in [manuscript §4](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/14_coupled_lattice.tex).

Every gap enters many cumulative distances, so this describes a genuinely coupled chain. If only a finite real block is known, we can use this formula for its contributions, while retaining the complete remaining exterior—including any nonreal zeros.

Your dipole interpretation also has a precise algebraic meaning. For target zeros \(a,b\), separated by \(g=b-a\), each exterior zero contributes
\[
\frac{1}{(\rho-b)(\rho-a)}
=
\frac1g\left(\frac1{\rho-b}-\frac1{\rho-a}\right).
\]
The difference on the right is the response of two opposite reciprocal-distance fields. Far away, their common leading contribution cancels: the difference decays like \(g/w^2\), where \(w\) is distance from the pair’s center. Thus **\(M\) is the summed dipole response per unit separation**. “Average” is a useful intuition, although there is no division by the number of exterior zeros.

And yes: higher orders give nearby zeros greater **relative weight**. In
\[
S_r=\sum_\rho (w_\rho^2-D)^{-r},
\]
a distant contribution decays like \(|w_\rho|^{-2r}\). Increasing \(p\) separately emphasizes proximity to one target pole; increasing \(q\) emphasizes proximity to the other.

A useful illustration is a perfectly uniform infinite chain with gap \(g\). The cumulative sums are \(L_m=R_m=mg\), giving \(M=2/g^2\). Consequently the gap law \(g'=4/g-2gM\) gives \(g'=0\): the pair’s mutual repulsion and the complete exterior contribution balance. The manuscript uses this stationary cosine example as a normalization check.

So I would sharpen my earlier preference this way: **estimate the coupled chain while preserving its shared dependencies, and read the desired \(D_n=g_n^2/4\) from that state.** Targeting a gap observable does not require treating the gap as an independent system.

The nonvanishing-factor statement concerns a different distinction: **what determines the zeros now, versus what determines their velocities**.

At a fixed time, write
\[
H(z)=Q(z)A(z),\qquad Q(z)=(z-a)(z-b),
\]
where \(A\) is analytic and nonzero throughout the disk surrounding the pair. Then
\[
\frac{H_z}{H}
=\frac1{z-a}+\frac1{z-b}+\frac{A_z}{A}.
\]
Because \(A_z/A\) is analytic inside the contour, its integrals against the polynomial weights \(1,z,z^2\) vanish. Those contour integrals therefore recover the pair’s count, center and squared gap entirely from \(Q\).

**But \(A_z/A\) need not be zero.** It disappears from those particular integrals; it remains present in the function and its derivatives.

Heat flow uses those derivatives. Since \(H_t=-H_{zz}\), differentiating \(H(t,x(t))=0\) at a simple zero gives
\[
x'=\frac{H_{zz}}{H_z}
=\frac{Q_{zz}}{Q_z}+2\frac{A_z}{A}
\quad\text{at }x.
\]
The extra term comes from the product-rule term \(2Q_zA_z\). Multiplying by \(A\) preserves the initial zero locations but can change the curvature relative to the slope at each zero—and therefore change its velocity.

Writing \(R=A_z/A\), the gap consequently satisfies
\[
g'=\frac4g+2\bigl[R(b)-R(a)\bigr],
\qquad
M=-\frac{R(b)-R(a)}g.
\]
This connects directly to your dipole picture: **the gap responds to the variation of the exterior field across the pair**. An equal velocity contribution at both roots changes the center alone.

For example, compare the initial fields
\[
Q(0,z)=z^2-1,\qquad
H(0,z)=(z^2-1)(z^2-25).
\]
Inside \(|z|=2\), both have exactly the pair \(-1,1\), hence \(D=1\). The extra factor is nonvanishing there. Yet evolving each full field by the same heat equation gives
\[
D_Q'(0)=2,\qquad D_H'(0)=\frac53.
\]
The exterior zeros at \(\pm5\) contribute \(M=1/12\), changing the second velocity through \(D'=2-4DM\).

A spatially constant normalization has \(A_z=0\) and never changes zero motion. A nonconstant local factor can encode the exterior influence even though it contributes nothing to the instantaneous pair-counting integrals.

I saved the derivations and checked example in [the brainstorm note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/brainstorm/notes/08_VCD_GT_CM_GAP_CHAIN_DIPOLE_AND_HEAT_FACTOR_DISCUSSION_20261118.md). The revised manuscript remains 107 pages, with a clean build and the edited pages visually checked.

:codex-file-citation{path="/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/output/pdf/vcd-complex-p-mellin/complex_power_evolution.pdf" purpose="output"}

I think a uniform infinite chain is definitely not the picture to have here. My understanding is that there is at least a basic (logarithmic) zeta height dependence that can be incorporated, so that should enter for even the simplest examples. I understand this is an illustration, but it might be oversimplified.

From the explanation, I don't think I'm getting the more nuanced picture, please continue.

You’re right: the uniform chain was too crude as the main picture. I’ll bring in the height-dependent zero density and distinguish the slow change in average spacing from local gap fluctuations. That should make clearer what \(M\) sees and where the difficult dynamics lie.

The manuscript already has the stronger picture in §15: an explicit height- and time-dependent reference spacing, with estimates for how actual zeros follow it on slabs bounded away from \(t=0\). I missed an important distinction in explaining this: the logarithmic density remains useful at time zero, but it does not make individual gaps nearly equal. The positive-time estimates that do give that stronger regularity lose their control as \(t\) approaches zero.

There is a more informative example in the existing certificate. Near height \(x=14010\), the smooth mean spacing is about \(1.79\), but the selected pair’s gap at time zero is only about \(0.0754\). Its exterior interaction is nevertheless close to the scale suggested by that density. This separates two things we need to track together: the surrounding density and the unusually small target gap.

The example also clarifies what higher moments detect: they exclude the two target zeros, so they can remain finite while that pair closes, provided the exterior stays separated. I also found the canonical version of the factor explanation in §15: a nonvanishing spatial envelope contributes a common leading velocity to high zeros, while the differences in their velocities govern the gaps.

You’re right. **The starting picture should be a nonuniform chain with a known density trend and substantial local fluctuations.** I gave too much prominence to a normalization check and too little to the canonical structure already in the manuscript.

The logarithmic height dependence enters immediately. In the manuscript’s coordinate \(x=2\gamma\), where \(\gamma\) is the usual zeta ordinate, the smooth counting density and corresponding reference spacing are
\[
\nu(X)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\log\frac{X}{4\pi},
\qquad
d(X)=\frac{4\pi}{\log(X/(4\pi))}.
\]
Thus the chain becomes progressively denser with height. These come from the smooth main term of the Riemann–von Mangoldt counting formula; they are **reference scales, not predictions for each individual gap**. [Rodgers–Tao, equations (38)–(39)](https://arxiv.org/html/1801.05914v5)

A useful representation is therefore
\[
g_n=d(X)\,\delta_n,\qquad M_n=d(X)^{-2}\,\mu_n.
\]
Here \(d(X)\) carries the known height dependence. The dimensionless quantities \(\delta_n\) and \(\mu_n\) carry the local configuration and its exterior interaction. Nothing in this change of units says that \(\delta_n\) is close to one.

This distinction matters because the exact gap law becomes
\[
\boxed{D_n'=2-\delta_n^2\mu_n.}
\]
It is the **combination of the target gap and its environment** that determines motion. Knowing the mean density—or even knowing that \(M_n\) has approximately its density-scale size—does not determine this combination.

There is a much better illustration than the uniform chain in the project’s existing canonical certificate. Near \(x=14010.16\), the reference spacing is about \(1.791\). For the selected pair, the recorded endpoint data give:

| Physical time \(t\) | Actual gap \(g\) | Gap relative to mean, \(g/d\) | Normalized exterior interaction, \(d^2M\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| \(0\) | \(0.075397\) | \(0.04210\) | \(1.9554\) |
| \(0.1\) | \(0.845546\) | \(0.47212\) | \(1.9366\) |

These are rounded readouts of the [existing certificate](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/numerics/16_VCD_GT_CM_EXTENDED_SOURCE_CERTIFICATE_20261118.json), not a new computation of the source.

The smooth density barely changes between these two times. The exterior interaction changes modestly. Yet the target gap changes dramatically.

At time zero, the surrounding interaction is quite close to its natural density scale, while the target gap is only **4.2% of the mean spacing**. Consequently,
\[
D'(0)\approx 2-(0.04210)^2(1.9554)\approx1.99653.
\]
The pair’s intrinsic separation term dominates. Increasing physical time opens this close pair rapidly; backward continuation reverses that motion. This is why a well-behaved surrounding density does not automatically protect an unusually small gap.

There is another important nuance in your higher-moment intuition: **the moments exclude the two target zeros**. Increasing their orders concentrates attention on nearby *exterior* zeros. If the target pair approaches a merger while all exterior zeros remain separated, \(M\) and every fixed higher exterior moment can remain finite. Their regularity does not prevent the merger. Their value is in distinguishing, for example, an isolated close pair from a larger crowded cluster—configurations with very different interactions.

The chain representation retains precisely that distinction. Each denominator uses cumulative neighboring gaps, so changing one gap changes many rows of the hierarchy. Replacing those cumulative distances by their averages before taking reciprocal products loses information: averaging a nonlinear reciprocal expression is not the same as evaluating it at average distances.

For practical estimates, the natural organization is therefore:

- A nearby block whose actual cumulative gaps are retained.
- A farther exterior controlled using the height-dependent counting density and its error bounds.
- Compatibility between the block, exterior and their evolution.

The distant zeros are individually weak contributors, as your dipole picture suggests, but their number grows with height. The complete tail must reflect that increasing population. Higher moments suppress distant contributions more strongly, while becoming more sensitive to the closest exterior geometry.

**The manuscript already does part of this in a specific regime.** In [§15, “Canonical comparisons on a fixed positive-time slab”](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/03_volterra_coefficient_dynamics/01_cluster_gap_transport/02_complex_p_mellin/manuscript/sections/13_canonical_time.tex), it uses a nonuniform, time-dependent reference clock \(G(q_n(t),t)=n\). Its local spacing is
